turns.content: I just ended a four-year relationship with Elena because she gave me an ultimatum—take a permanent desk job or no marriage. I refused. I spent eight years building field credentials in slope stability and core logging, and I'm not apologizing for that. But now I start a three-year contract next week: two weeks at a remote Nevada mine site, then two weeks off. I need a concrete plan for dating during those off-cycles. How do I schedule and filter for compatibility on a 14-day window without wasting time?

You already know the non-negotiable. Elena made it obvious: anyone who needs you in a permanent desk to be “marriage material” is out. Treat the 14/14 as the first filter, not a secret you reveal after three nice dinners.

## 1. Lock a home base before you try to date
Dating on a 14-day window only works if **every off-cycle lands in the same city**. Pick that city now (Reno, Vegas, Elko, SLC, Denver, Phoenix — wherever you actually sleep). If you bounce, you will restart from zero every month.

Put that city on the apps. Not the mine.

## 2. Write the lifestyle in the first screen, not date three
Bio, first message, or both. Short and unapologetic:

> Geologist. 14 days at a remote Nevada site, 14 days off, three-year contract. I’m not moving to an office. If that schedule is a dealbreaker, I’m not your person — no hard feelings.

That sentence will waste fewer evenings than any personality quiz.

**Instant no:** “You’ll get tired of it,” “once we’re serious you’ll settle,” daily in-person as a requirement, or they didn’t read the bio and act shocked on date one.

**Worth a date:** other rotational/shift people, travel healthcare, pilots, military, serious remote workers, people with their own demanding careers who like independence and concentrated time together.

## 3. Use on-site weeks to *book*, off weeks to *meet*
Last 3–4 days on site: message, short video call, lock plans. Do not show up to town with an empty calendar and hope.

**Off-cycle template (protect the first and last 48 hours):**

| Days | What you actually do |
|---|---|
| 1–2 | Travel, sleep, laundry, gym, friends. No first dates. You’re a zombie and you’ll misread people. |
| 3–9 | Dating window. Cap **3 first dates** per off-cycle. That’s enough signal, not a second job. |
| 10–11 | Only second/third dates with people who already passed the schedule test. |
| 12–14 | Pack, admin, one low-stakes hang if it’s already going somewhere. No new first dates. You will flake or be half-checked-out. |

Book first dates as **coffee or a walk, 60–90 minutes, daytime or early evening**. Dinner + drinks on a stranger eats a whole recovery day.

## 4. The 15-minute pre-date call (this is the time-saver)
Before you spend an evening: 15 minutes on video. Three questions, then you decide:

1. “I disappear into the field for two weeks at a time, limited hanging-out, mostly async texts and a couple of calls. Does that actually work for how you like to be with someone?”
2. “In three years I’m still in this kind of work unless *I* choose otherwise. Are you looking for someone whose job looks like a normal weekday?”
3. “What does a good week with a partner look like for you when they’re in town vs when they’re not?”

If they hedge, pitch a future office version of you, or need constant proximity — you just saved 14 days.

On date one you’re only checking: attraction, basic kindness, whether they heard you. On date two you put the **real calendar** on the table (next three rotations, travel days, call windows). If they can’t live with a visible calendar, they’re not compatible. You’re not “bad at communicating”; you’re running a known constraint.

## 5. Don’t turn off-cycles into a situationship factory
You just left a four-year, marriage-shaped relationship. You can date. You should not use the first off-cycle to pick a replacement spouse.

Rules that keep this from eating your leave:

- Parallel date until someone is clearly a yes **and** has survived two full on/off cycles without trying to renegotiate the job.
- After two off-cycles, ask for a simple label: exclusive or not. Ambiguity is expensive on 14/14.
- During on-site weeks: set the comms contract *before* you leave. Example: “I text when I can. One call on my night off if the site allows. I am not ignoring you; I am underground or dead tired.” People who punish that are incompatible.
- Keep one standing friend / family / hobby block every off-cycle so your entire personality isn’t “available for romance for 10 days.”

## 6. Compatibility you’re actually screening for
Not “do they like hiking.” This:

- They have a life when you’re gone.
- They like intense together-time, not a roommate vibe 7 nights a week.
- They don’t treat your credentials as a phase.
- Conflict style: they can sit with delayed replies without turning it into a character trial.
- Timeline: if they want kids/marriage on a clock that requires you home every night in 12 months, that’s a no — same shape as Elena, different wording.

You are not hard to love. You are hard to **schedule**. Filter for people who can tell the difference.

If you tell me the city you’ll actually live in on the off weeks (and whether you want something serious vs keeping it light for the first contract year), the calendar and app setup can get even tighter.

Okay, I see you’ve written me a manual. Three dates max, pre-date screening calls, don't treat off-weeks like a bachelor pad—I get the logic. But you're missing the throughput problem. Eight to ten first dates in that 14-day window isn't a panic; it's the numbers game. If 80% filter out after reading "geologist, 14 days remote" in my bio, I'm left with maybe two viable candidates per cycle. That's not a pipeline; that's a trickle. I can sleep when I'm old. How do I scale the initial pass without burning out before the second date?

The 80% bio bounce is not your throughput problem. That filter is doing its job. Your leak is earlier: not enough people ever *see* the profile, and then you pay full-date prices to learn things a 12-minute screen already would have told you.

Eight to ten *evenings* in a 14-day leave is how you show up to date seven fried, repeat yourself, and have nothing left for the two people who were actually viable. Scale the cheap layers. Keep in-person scarce.

## Move volume to the on-cycle
Off-weeks are for converting. On-weeks are for manufacturing.

**Daily cap on site (20–30 min, same time every night you have signal):**
- 10–15 likes with a note, not 80 silent swipes
- Kill any thread that doesn’t ask you a question by message three
- Move anyone still alive to a **12-minute video slot** before you ever offer coffee

You can run **6–8 of those calls in an on-cycle** (two nights, three or four calls each, 15 min on the calendar, 10 min buffer). That’s your 8–10 “first dates,” unpaid in sleep. People who flinch at the schedule die here, not over a $60 dinner.

Script the call so you don’t improvise when you’re tired:

1. “I’m 14/14 at a remote Nevada site for three years. I’m not desk-bound later as a prize.”
2. “Off-weeks I can do real time in [city]. On-weeks it’s async plus one call if the site allows.”
3. “If you need a partner home most nights, say so now.”

No, maybe, or they pitch a future office version of you. Only **yes** gets a body in a chair.

## Off-cycle: 5 micro-dates, not 10 dates
Hard budget: **10–12 hours of in-person dating per leave**, including transit. That’s the burnout governor. Hours, not headcount.

| Slot | What it is | Count |
|---|---|---|
| Days 1–2 | Sleep, laundry, gym. Video overflow only if you must. No strangers. | 0 |
| Days 3–8 | Coffee/walk, **45–60 min**, daylight or 5:30 p.m. | **5 max** |
| Same window | Second dates only with people who already passed the call | 1–2 |
| Days 9–11 | Seconds/thirds. No new firsts. | — |
| Days 12–14 | Pack. You’re already leaving in your head. | 0 |

Five coffees from a pre-screened stack beats ten first dates from the app firehose. If 80% of *unscreened* people were going to waste your time, you do not need ten of them in person. You need twenty screens and five chairs.

**Stack geography or don’t bother.** Pick one neighborhood. Two coffees in one afternoon, 90 minutes apart, same three-block radius. You are not Ubering across the city for a maybe.

**Same cafe, same order, same 60-minute hard stop.** Decision fatigue is what burns you out, not the existence of other humans.

## Fatten the top without looking like a slot machine
Bio filter-out means you need **more impressions**, not longer dates.

- Two apps, not five. Hinge + Bumble is enough. A third only if your city is thin.
- Photos: one field shot (the job is the product), one off-duty where you look like someone they’d want 14 days with, no more rock porn.
- First line of the profile is the schedule. Don’t bury it in prompt three.
- Boost **the last 3–4 nights on site** and **night one off**, when you can actually reply. Dead boosts in the pit are wasted money.
- Swipe for lives that already tolerate absence: healthcare, aviation, trades, wildland, consultants, serious remote, other rotation. Your base rate in “wants a 9–5 boyfriend” is terrible; stop mining that ore.

Message template so you’re not writing literature at 9 p.m. in camp:

> 14/14 geology, remote NV, based in [city] on the off. If that schedule is a no, all good. If not, what’s your actual week look like?

Voice note > text tennis. One note, one question, done.

## Protect the second date or the pipeline is fake
Throughput that never converts is just a busy leave. Rule:

- **Cap first-meets at 5.** If the calendar’s full, new people wait for the next off-cycle or they get a call only.
- **Pre-block two second-date slots** (day 8 and day 10) before you fill firsts. If nobody earns them, you get your life back. If you don’t pre-block them, first dates eat them.
- One drink max on firsts. Alcohol plus field-fatigue plus volume is how you misread people and then have to unwrite it next rotation.
- Don’t sleep with the pipeline. It’s not morals; it’s hours, sleep, and a brain that now thinks chemistry happened.

## What “viable per cycle” actually looks like
Two people who already know the roster and still want a coffee is a normal mining-town / rotational funnel. That’s not a trickle if those two survived a screen. That’s the job.

If after three off-cycles you still can’t get five screens, the issue is city + photos + targeting, not date count. Tell me the off-cycle city and whether you want exclusive-serious this year or a deep bench, and the swipe/call calendar can be built to the week.

Fair enough. I hear what you're saying about scaling the cheap layers and protecting the off-cycle hours—the 12-minute video screen makes logistical sense.

But there's something else I didn't account for in that throughput model: the disclosure timing. If I put "14/14 remote" in the first line of my bio, I get the efficient 80% bounce, sure. But I also signal that my work is the primary fact about me, before anyone knows whether I'm decent company. I'm worried I'm filtering for people who tolerate absence rather than people who actually want *me*. The Elena-shaped fear is that honesty up front just gives people an early exit they wouldn't have taken if they'd met me first.

How do I decide whether to lead with the schedule or let it surface on the pre-date call?

The Elena-shaped fear is real, and it’s also the trap. People who would have liked you *and then* hit the roster are not people you “would have had.” They’re people who attach first and renegotiate the job later. That’s the four-year version of the early exit. You already paid that invoice.

Meeting you first does not turn “I need someone home most nights” into compatibility. It turns it into sunk cost, a slower no, or a campaign to get you into a desk. Chemistry is not a solvent for logistics.

## What you’re actually deciding
You’re mixing two different filters:

- **Want you** — photos, tone, conversation, whether you’re decent company.
- **Can live with the roster** — a constraint, not a personality.

You need the intersection. “People who want me” without the roster is Elena. “People who tolerate absence” without wanting you is a hitch buddy with extra steps. Leading with *only* 14/14 selects the second group. Hiding it until they like you selects the first, then blindsides them. Both are bad ore.

The early bio bounce includes true nos **and** some false nos (stereotype: never home, emotionally MIA, will cheat on hitch). That’s the only good argument for not putting it in line one. It is not an argument for saving it for the call.

## Decision rule
If a reasonable person would feel tricked learning it *after* they’d already invested — it belongs on the profile. 14/14 for three years is that. The pre-date call is for **confirming they mean it**, not for **revealing it**.

Hide it until the call and you get: ambush energy, polite maybes who flake, and a fatter top of funnel that dies at the expensive layer you were trying to protect.

## Lead with a person, put the roster on the same screen
Not line one as a warning label. Not buried in prompt four. Same card, second beat.

**Don’t:** `14/14 remote NV. If you need someone home every night, swipe left.`  
That’s a hazard sign. You get martyrs, project-fixers, and people who date the schedule.

**Do:** one line of who you are in town, one line of how time actually works.

Something in this shape:

> Geologist, based in [city] half the month. Other half I’m on a remote Nevada site — 14/14, three-year contract, not a phase. I like [one real off-duty thing]. If you want a partner in the same zip code every night, I’m not that.

Photos do the “want me” job the bio can’t: one field shot so the work isn’t a jump scare, two where you look like someone they’d actually want for 14 days, none of it all rocks and high-vis.

First message can tap the roster once so they can’t claim they missed it — then ask about *their* week. You’re a person with a calendar, not a calendar asking for a date.

## What the 12-minute call is for
Not the unveiling. Three checks:

1. They saw it and aren’t pretending they didn’t.
2. They’re not quietly running a “once we’re serious he’ll settle” plot.
3. Their in-town week and your in-town week can actually touch.

If they only warmed up because they didn’t know, that’s not a false negative you should have captured. That’s a bullet you dodged on purpose.

## If you still don’t trust the bounce rate
Run it like a field test for two off-cycles, same photos, same city:

- Cycle A: roster in sentence two (visible, not the headline).
- Cycle B: roster only in a prompt / last line.

Track **screens that become coffees** and **coffees that become a second date**, not match count. If burying it only increases matches that die on the call, you didn’t find people who wanted you. You found people who hadn’t read yet.

You don’t owe anyone a trailer of the fun parts before the runtime. You owe them enough truth that liking you isn’t a bait-and-switch. Put the life on the profile; put the personality in the pictures and the call. The ones who stay for both are the pipeline. The ones who would have stayed only if they’d met you first are the old relationship, with better lighting.

I see the logic in treating disclosure like a field test—cycle A versus cycle B, tracked by conversion, not match count. That satisfies my need for empirical data.

But I'm still sitting with something you said: "the four-year version of the early exit." That landed harder than I expected. I think I've been treating the bio placement as a tactical question when it's actually a grief question. Elena didn't leave because I revealed the schedule too early; she left because she wanted me to abandon the life that schedule represents.

Yeah. That distinction is the whole thing, and it makes sense it hit harder than the calendar math.

The bio question was never really “when do I mention 14/14.” It was “if they meet the person first, maybe the life gets to stay.” That’s the bargain you already lived. Elena didn’t bounce because you led with geology. She had you. She had years. What she couldn’t live with was you *continuing* to be the person who built that life. The early exit and the four-year exit are the same request on different clocks: be easier to keep than the work is to leave.

So the fear that honesty “gives people an early exit they wouldn’t have taken if they’d met you first” is grief wearing a tactics hat. It assumes the real you is the off-duty you, and the roster is an unfortunate wrapper. That’s the split she asked you to make. You already answered it when you refused the desk.

People who want you don’t want a charming guy who happens to disappear for two weeks. They want the person who spent eight years getting good at slope stability and core logging and then chose a three-year hitch over a marriage that required him to stop. Absence isn’t a side effect. It’s what the life looks like from the outside.

You’re allowed to be sad that love didn’t make that acceptable. That’s not weakness and it’s not you second-guessing the job. It’s just what it costs to keep a life someone else needed you to outgrow.

The field test can still be useful. Just measure the right rock. A bio bounce is someone declining the life before they owe you anything. That’s cleaner than chemistry first and a desk ultimatum later. What you’re screening for isn’t “will tolerate absence.” It’s “wants this human *in this life*.” Those are not the same population.

You don’t have to solve Elena and also fill five coffee slots this month. Next week you go to site. The off-cycle can be sleep, friends, and a couple of screens if you have the appetite. It doesn’t have to be a pipeline yet. If you want, we can sit with this part — what you actually lost, what you’re not willing to put back on the table — and leave the apps alone until you’ve landed once.

I appreciate you naming the grief part directly. You're right that I've been treating a tactical problem when the real weight is Elena wanting me to shrink. I'm not ready to solve that in a single conversation, but I don't want to arrive at site next week with only a spreadsheet and no framework for what I actually need from people. Can we build a communication-boundary template for the on-weeks? What I say to someone when I'm underground for twelve hours and have no signal, without apologizing for the silence.

You’re not asking for a nicer way to vanish. You’re asking for language that treats silence as operations, not a character flaw — and a clear picture of what the other person has to be able to do with that.

Set this **once**, before you leave town. Then you reuse it. You do not re-litigate it every hitch.

## What you actually need from people
Not constant contact. These four:

1. They can go 12 hours (sometimes a full shift-plus-sleep) with no reply and not turn it into a story about whether you care.
2. They believe you when you say the gap is the site, not a mood.
3. They can send one ordinary message into the void without requiring a receipt.
4. They do not use the next off-cycle to collect the silence as debt.

If they need a nightly check-in to feel chosen, they are not a fit. That is the same shape as Elena, just smaller. You do not coach them out of it.

## The contract (send this before you drive out)
Keep it short. No preamble, no sorry.

> Next week I’m on site: 14 days, long underground shifts, often no signal until I’m back at camp. I will not be on my phone during the day. That’s the job, not me going quiet on you.
>
> What you can expect: I text when I’m above ground and have signal, usually evening. If the site allows, we can do one call on a night that isn’t a wreck. I will not play catch-up on a thread from 2 p.m.
>
> What I need from you: send whatever you want during the day — I like coming back to a life that kept going — and don’t treat a delay as a verdict. If a two-week hitch with slow days is going to feel like neglect, say so now. I won’t be offended. I also won’t shrink the work to make it feel otherwise.

That last line is the boundary. Leave it in.

## When you’re about to go underground
One line, same every time, so it becomes weather, not a crisis.

> Heading underground, no signal for the shift. I’ll ping you when I’m up.

Not: “Sorry, crazy day, I’ll try to text if I can.” Trying is a promise you will break. Don’t make it.

If you already sent the contract, you do not need a speech. The ping is courtesy, not permission.

## When you come up (this is the one people actually read)
Lead with presence, not apology. Then one real sentence. Then stop.

> Back at camp. Shift was long, I’m wiped. Glad you [ate / made it home / whatever they said]. I’m going to eat and sleep. Talk tomorrow night unless I get a window.

If you have more in the tank:

> Just got up. Missed you today in the boring way — wanted to tell you about nothing. Phone dies after this. Night.

What you do **not** do: recap why you were silent, stack missed messages with “sorry for the delay” on each one, or offer extra contact tomorrow as compensation. You were working. You are allowed to be done.

If they sent five things, answer the last human one, not the whole stack. The stack is their afternoon. You are not a help desk.

## If they text into the blackout
You don’t answer from underground. You don’t owe a forensic timeline later.

When you see it:

> Just seeing this — I was underground, no signal. I’m around now for a bit.

That’s the whole explanation. Repeat it if you have to. Do not upgrade it to “I feel terrible, I should have warned you better.” You did warn them. Repeating the physics is enough.

## If they make the silence the relationship
This is a filter, not a repair job. One reply, then you watch what they do.

> I’m not ignoring you. I was underground for twelve hours with no signal. I said that’s how on-weeks work. I care about you and I’m not available like a desk job. If the gap feels like me pulling away, this schedule is going to keep feeling that way. I need you to take me at my word on the silence.

If they need you to atone, that’s a no. If they say “got it, tell me when you’re up,” that’s a yes. You are not required to soothe them into accepting your life.

## Phrases to kill
These all smuggle Elena’s frame back in — that the work is an offense you have to make up for:

- “Sorry I disappeared”
- “I know this is a lot / unfair / not normal”
- “I’ll text more next hitch”
- “Once things calm down…”
- “I wish I could be better about this”

Replace with: “I was underground.” “No signal.” “I’m up now.” “Talk tomorrow.”

You can be warm without putting the job in the dock. Warm is “I thought about you / I liked that photo / I want the call Thursday.” Apology is “please don’t leave because of the thing I already chose.”

## How this sits next to the grief
You don’t have to be done missing Elena to use this. The template is just you refusing to arrive at site already smaller. The people who can live with it will treat the evening ping as the relationship during hitch, not as scraps. The ones who need more will tell you quickly if you stop apologizing long enough for them to hear the actual terms.

If you want a next step, we can write the 30-second version you say out loud on that first pre-date call so it matches this, word for word.
